NeuroTranslate 0.0 · Muscle and motion

A walking-trained forecast did not carry over to standing

People stood or walked while the visual scene around them turned. A marker on the bone at the base of the spine (the sacrum) tracked the pelvis, and skin electrodes recorded the electrical activity of four muscles in each lower leg (EMG, a muscle recording, not a nerve recording). The forecast covers the next eighth of a second of both.

On 879 standing events from six people the models never saw, the forecast learned from walking alone missed the muscle signals by 10.54 µV, against 5.34 µV for one learned from standing. Simply continuing the last movement and holding the muscle amplitude did best of all (4.78 µV, 0.65 mm). Keep an invented history fixed below and change which recordings taught the model.

What was transferred?

One model learned a relationship between past readings and future changes using only walking recordings. A second started with that relationship and adjusted its coefficients using the first third of each development participant’s standing rotation log. A third learned from those same standing examples starting from zero. All three issue forecasts for a different person without seeing that person’s future.

Averaging the eight muscle errors gives a value in microvolts. The motion score averages the distance between predicted and observed markers at each of 32 future samples. Comparing only the final position could miss an earlier turn in the path. Neither these filtered recordings nor their forecasts establish the time required for a biological signal to travel.
